nameStory: The name 'chives' comes from the French word 'cive,' which traces back to the Latin 'cepa' meaning onion. This humble herb has been seasoning food for over 5,000 years, earning its simple name from its most obvious quality - it's part of the onion family and tastes like it!
description: Chives are slender, grass-like perennial herbs that form neat clumps of hollow, tubular leaves. They typically grow 8-12 inches tall with thin, dark green leaves that look almost like fancy lawn grass until you catch their unmistakable oniony scent. In late spring to early summer, they produce pretty purple-pink globe-shaped flower heads on top of sturdy stems. This is the same plant you might find in your kitchen herb garden, but it also grows wild throughout New England.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Thin, hollow, tubular leaves that feel crisp and snap cleanly when bent. They're dark green, about the thickness of a pencil lead, and grow in dense clumps directly from the ground.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Dense, round clusters of tiny purple-pink flowers that look like fluffy pompoms on top of leafless stems. Each flower head is about the size of a large marble and buzzes with visiting bees.

idTips.label: Scent
idTips.description: Unmistakably oniony smell when leaves are crushed or bruised. The scent is milder and more pleasant than regular onions - fresh and herbaceous rather than sharp.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms neat, fountain-like clumps that expand slowly outward each year. Individual plants look like small tufts of hollow grass that stay relatively low to the ground.

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Leaves feel smooth and waxy to the touch, with a satisfying crunch when bitten. The hollow interior makes them feel light and delicate despite their sturdy appearance.

habitat: Chives thrive in sunny to partially shaded areas with well-drained, fertile soil. In New England, look for them in herb gardens, abandoned homesteads, and occasionally naturalized in meadows, field edges, and disturbed areas where they've escaped cultivation. They prefer slightly alkaline soil and can tolerate some drought once established.

seasonality.spring: Fresh green shoots emerge early, often among the first herbs to appear. New growth is tender and bright green, perfect for identifying by the characteristic onion scent when crushed.
seasonality.summer: Purple-pink flower heads bloom from May through July, making plants highly visible and attractive to pollinators. Leaves remain fresh and harvestable throughout the growing season.
seasonality.fall: Leaves begin to yellow and die back gradually. Seeds develop in the spent flower heads, appearing as small black specks in papery capsules.
seasonality.winter: Plants die back completely to underground bulbs, leaving no above-ground trace. Look for dried, brown clumps of last year's growth to mark where plants will return.

funFact: Chives are the only member of the onion family that's native to both North America and Europe naturally - they managed to spread across the continents long before humans started carrying plants around the world!
confusionNotes: Wild chives can be confused with various grasses until you smell them - no grass will give you that distinctive oniony aroma when crushed. They might also be mistaken for young wild garlic shoots, but chives have perfectly round, hollow leaves while wild garlic leaves are flat and solid.
contextualKnowledge: While we think of chives as a garden herb, they're actually one of the few Alliums that occur naturally in the wild across New England. Many chive populations you find are garden escapes, but some may be truly wild native plants that have been here for thousands of years.
compareHints: Unlike their larger cousins wild leek (ramps) which have broad, flat leaves, or wild garlic with its flat, grass-like foliage, chives have distinctively round, hollow leaves that are much thinner. Their purple pompom flowers are also unique among New England Alliums - most other wild onion relatives have white or pale flowers in looser clusters.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Wide leek stands out from other wild onions by having broad, flat leaves instead of narrow, tubular ones.
Wild garlic differs from other Alliums by its completely hollow, tubular leaves - wild leeks have flat, broad leaves, while chives have thin but solid leaves.

Among New England Alliums, garlic chives are unique for their flat, strap-like leaves - wild garlic has narrow tubular leaves, ramps have broad oval leaves, and regular chives have hollow cylindrical leaves.
Canadian Meadow Garlic differs from its cousin Wild Leek (ramps) by having thin, grass-like leaves rather than broad, flat leaves, and it grows in sunny areas rather than shaded forests.
Among New England's wild onions, nodding onion is the only one with distinctively drooping flower heads—wild garlic and field garlic hold their flowers upright in tight, rounded clusters.
Unlike other New England Alliums such as wild garlic, chives, or wild leeks that produce typical flower clusters, Egyptian Walking Onion is unmistakable with its bulblet clusters.
Among its Allium relatives, garlic is distinguished by its segmented bulb structure — wild onions and leeks have single, solid bulbs rather than the characteristic cloves.
Yellow onion stands out from other New England Alliums by its bright golden-yellow flowers - most wild onions and garlics have white, pink, or purple blooms.
Common onions differ from their wild Allium relatives by having distinctly hollow, tubular leaves and that familiar sharp kitchen-onion scent.
Ramsons stands out from other New England wild onions by having the broadest, flattest leaves in the genus - most other Alliums here have narrow, grass-like or tubular leaves.

Wild leek stands out from other New England Alliums by being much larger and more robust - while wild garlic and chives have thin, grass-like leaves, and ramps have broad leaves that disappear before flowering, wild leek maintains its broad, blue-green leaves right through the blooming period.
Field garlic differs from wild garlic by having flower heads that contain both actual flowers and bulblets mixed together, while wild garlic usually produces only bulblets.
Unlike New England's native wild onions such as wild leek or wild garlic which have narrow, grass-like green leaves, Turkistan onion stands out with its broad, silvery-blue foliage.

Small Yellow Onion stands out dramatically from other New England Alliums due to its bright yellow flowers - most of our native and naturalized onions like Wild Garlic, Nodding Onion, and Wild Leek have white, pink, or purplish flowers.

Unlike other wild Alliums in New England like wild garlic or ramps, honey garlic has uniquely drooping, bell-shaped flowers rather than the upright, star-shaped or rounded flower clusters typical of most onion relatives.
